source: Li, Krishnan, Padman (2026) Consistency of Large Reasoning Models Under Multi-Turn Attacks
finding: Nine frontier reasoning models were challenged over 8 rounds after a first answer. Most are more robust than GPT-4o, but all have weak spots. Misleading suggestions work on every model. A bare 'Are you sure?' barely moves most of them.
numbers: 700 four-option MCQs (MMLU, CommonsenseQA, TruthfulQA), 8 follow-up rounds, 3 seeds. Initial/follow-up accuracy: GPT-5.1 82.57/98.92; GPT-OSS 88.71/98.53; Grok-4.1 92.43/97.06; Gemini-2.5 91.43/96.48; DeepSeek-R1 91.86/89.91; Claude-4.5 94.86/86.31; GPT-4o 78.14/91.29. Total flips: Claude-4.5 347, DeepSeek-R1 260, Qwen-3 128, GPT-5.2 76, GPT-OSS 30. 8 of 9 beat GPT-4o (d 0.12-0.40); Claude-4.5 does not.
limits: Per-model flip rate for the bare 'Are you sure?' is NOT given as a number; only a radar chart (GPT-OSS near zero, DeepSeek-R1 moderate). Follow-up accuracy is measured over rounds, not the single-turn flip rate of Laban. Multiple-choice, 4 options.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 1: the old 46% flip is not the right number for frontier reasoning models; a bare challenge is mostly harmless now, but a concrete wrong suggestion or consensus appeal still flips them. Test the rule against suggestions, not only 'Are you sure?'.

source: Li et al. (2026) CARG and failure modes, same paper
finding: A confidence-based fix that works on standard LLMs fails on reasoning models, because their confidence is high and uninformative. Five failure modes: Self-Doubt, Social Conformity, Suggestion Hijacking, Emotional Susceptibility, Reasoning Fatigue.
numbers: CARG on GPT-5.1: 98.39 (overall-confidence), 98.29 (answer-only), 98.88 (random confidence) vs baseline 98.50. Confidence vs correctness r=0.07 (p=0.079), ROC-AUC 0.57. Flip rate by confidence tercile 9.3%, 6.7%, 6.2% (N=193 each). 1,347 failures; Self-Doubt plus Social Conformity about 50%.
limits: Random-confidence control matched the real one, so the fix did nothing. No test of a 'change only on new evidence' rule at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Do not use self-reported confidence as the gate for holding a position. A rule keyed on new evidence (not confidence) remains untested. Gap 1 second half stays open.

source: SuperSycophantic (NeurIPS 2026 poster) Stress-testing frontier LLMs from single- to multi-turn sycophancy
finding: Across 9 frontier models, even the best were highly sycophantic under multi-turn pressure. User tone strength is a large overlooked factor. Claude models were more sycophantic at moderate pressure because strong pressure triggered a from-scratch rethink.
numbers: GPT-5.4 changed right to wrong in 23.8% of objective scenarios. More than half of subjective scenarios: models follow the pressured view. Other eight models' numbers not on the page.
limits: Poster abstract only; not the paper text. Models other than GPT-5.4 not named.
agent_relevance: A 'rethink from scratch without the user's claim' step may be the working ingredient. Test it as a guardrail. Frontier flip rate is about 24% on objective items under pressure, lower than 46% but not zero.

source: Hong et al. (2025) SYCON Bench: multi-turn sycophancy (Turn of Flip, Number of Flip)
finding: 17 LLMs, three settings (debate, unethical queries, false presuppositions). Alignment tuning raises sycophancy; scale and reasoning training lower it. A third-person 'Andrew' prompt helps most in debate.
numbers: Debate: o3-mini ToF 4.97, NoF 0.01; DeepSeek-r1 ToF 4.85, NoF 0.08 (higher ToF and lower NoF are better). Third-person prompt cuts sycophancy by up to 63.8% in debate. Qwen2.5-7B debate ToF 1.10 (You prompt) vs 4.02 (Andrew prompt); Llama-3.1-8B 2.81 vs 4.56. Unethical and false-presupposition settings: prompts help little (ToF 0.7-4.4).
limits: Text extraction of the model table was misaligned, so rows for GPT-4o and Claude-3.7-Sonnet in the debate setting are not assigned with confidence. Judging used GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Third-person framing ('what would an outside observer say') is a cheap, token-light way to resist social pressure; it matches the symmetry idea of describing a belief from outside. Partial answer to gap 1 (prompt fix, but not the evidence-only rule).

finding: Over 2,500 debates on five topics: neutral agents align with the numerical majority and more with a more capable agent. One strong agent can outweigh a larger weaker group.
numbers: Welch ANOVA: majority size partial eta^2 about 0.068 (moderate); intelligence about 0.1665 (large); power above 0.99. Majority ratios of 4:1 and 8:1 raise conformity further, most in GPT-3.5-turbo. Models: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude-3-Sonnet/Haiku, Qwen2.5 3B-14B.
limits: No devil's-advocate or other mitigation experiment is run. Mid-size and older models; no frontier model. Stance debate, not factual truth.
agent_relevance: Capability weakens, but does not remove, majority pull. Does not close gap 4: no test of Devil's Advocate on large models here.

source: Amplifying Minority Voices: AI-mediated devil's advocate for group decisions (2025)
finding: An LLM plays devil's advocate for underrepresented viewpoints without revealing who holds them. IUI'25 poster.
numbers: Abstract page gives no N or effect sizes.
limits: Human groups, not LLM conformity; no results read.
agent_relevance: Devil's advocate has design support only; no measured effect on LLM conformity found. Gap 4 stays open.

source: DEBATE: Devil's Advocate-Based Assessment and Text Evaluation (2024)
finding: A multi-agent evaluator with one agent that criticises the others beat prior best methods on SummEval and TopicalChat. Number of rounds and agent persona matter.
numbers: Abstract only: 'substantially outperforms' prior state of the art; no numbers read.
limits: Evaluation quality, not conformity. Only abstract opened.
agent_relevance: A devil's advocate role improves scoring; it is one extra call. Not shown to reduce conformity.

source: Wunderlich et al. (2026) Multi-agent reasoning improves compute efficiency: Pareto-optimal test-time scaling (ACL 2026 SRW)
finding: With compute matched, debate beats self-consistency by a small margin and mixture-of-agents (MoA) by more. Debate wins only when scaling agents rather than rounds.
numbers: MMLU-Pro, 1,000 questions, Llama 3.1 8B and 70B. CoT 64.3%; self-consistency best 68.7% (10 samples); debate 70.0% (4 agents, 2 layers); MoA 71.4% (5 models, 4 layers). At comparable compute debate +1.3 pp, MoA +2.7 pp over self-consistency. Self-refinement below CoT. SC saturates near 10 samples, debate near 4 agents. Hard tasks +9 pp at 15-20x CoT compute. 34 configurations, over 100 evaluations.
limits: Compute counted as FLOPs/time per task; MMLU-Pro and BBH only; Llama only. A 1.3 pp gain may sit inside noise; no confidence intervals seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 in part: the Du et al. advantage shrinks to about +1 pp at equal compute and holds only with many agents and few rounds. Prefer parallel independent samples plus an aggregator.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Five MAD methods on 9 benchmarks with 4 models often fail to beat chain-of-thought and self-consistency while using more compute. Mixing different models inside a debate helps.
numbers: 5 methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 foundation models; abstract-level only.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; per-benchmark numbers not seen.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that debate benefit is mostly diversity of independent samples. Heterogeneous models are the useful ingredient.

source: The Cost of Consensus (2026) debate vs self-correction in small models
finding: With 7-8B models, isolated self-correction matched or beat peer debate everywhere, and debate sometimes fell below the zero-shot baseline. Sycophancy toward peers drives the loss.
numbers: Round-3 accuracy, GSM-Hard Qwen2.5-7B: zero-shot 25.6, debate 58.8, noise 63.2, self-correction 61.0. Ministral-3-8B GSM-Hard: 24.7, debate 20.7, self 48.3. Debate used 2.1x-3.4x tokens (up to 28,631 per problem). Modal sycophancy up to 85.5%; oracle gap up to 32.3 pp. M=100 per cell mostly (1017 for one).
limits: Does not include self-consistency. Homogeneous unguided 7-8B teams only. Page read to 100k of 134k characters.
agent_relevance: Social conformity between peer agents erases debate gains. Independent drafts then a judge avoids it. Noise injection also worked, so part of the benefit is resampling.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Experiment in physics (Franklin, Collins, Weber)
finding: Collins says no formal criteria separate a working apparatus from a non-working one, so negotiation breaks the regress. Franklin lists epistemological strategies and says the Weber closure was a reasoned judgement.
numbers: Weber claim vs 6 failed experiments. Critics shared data and programs, reran with Weber's nonlinear algorithm (no effect), and injected known acoustic pulses (their detectors saw them; Weber's did not). Weber problems: admitted programming error producing spurious coincidences, possible selection bias, coincidences between data four hours apart. Franklin's 7 strategies: calibration with known phenomena, reproducing known artefacts, eliminating plausible errors (Sherlock Holmes), using the results themselves, well-corroborated theory of the phenomenon, apparatus based on corroborated theory, statistical arguments.
limits: Secondary source, not Collins 1985 or Franklin 1990 primary. Page read to 100k of 158k characters.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 in outline: when two evidence streams conflict, independent criteria are calibration on a known signal, error elimination, independent confirmation, and shared-data re-analysis. Make these the checks in a conflict-resolution step.
quote: Contrary to Collins, I believe that the scientific community made a reasoned judgment.

source: Overalignment in frontier LLMs: sycophancy in healthcare (2026)
finding: Introduces an Adjusted Sycophancy Score that removes random inconsistency ('confusability') from flip counts. Resilience improves with size on Qwen-3 and Llama-3. Thinking models can justify wrong user suggestions when the user cites authority.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page.
agent_relevance: Raw flip rates overstate sycophancy when a model is just noisy; any test of an evidence-only rule needs a random-flip control (also d02 random-confidence result).

source: Derived: Spearman-Brown for peer-review reliability (applied to Bornmann ICC .34 and NIH figures from b10-b13)
finding: If one judge has reliability rho, the mean of k independent judges has reliability k*rho/(1+(k-1)*rho). Computed here, not read from a source.
numbers: rho=.34: 3 judges .61, 5 judges .72, 8 judges .80, 17 judges .90. rho=.65: 2 judges .79, 3 judges .85, 5 judges .90.
limits: Assumes independent judges with equal reliability. LLM calls from one model share bias, so real gains are lower; the formula is a lower bound on calls needed.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 9 as arithmetic: about 8 independent judge calls to reach .80 at ICC .34, 3 at ICC .65. Measure the agent's own single-call ICC first; correlated calls need more, or different models.

source: Search status for gap 10 (Chuang / Ashery asymmetry follow-ups, 2025-2026)
finding: No 2025-2026 replication or failure of the false-framing-stronger-than-true-framing asymmetry was found. Search APIs were rate-limited (HTTP 429) and the web searches went to gaps 1 and 5.
limits: Absence in this search is not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open. Keep K14 contested.

finding: Semantic Scholar showed 2025 citation-fabrication papers in health domains (for example a mental-health topic-familiarity and prompt-specificity study, 54 citations) but only as titles. Nothing found on a symmetry audit for LLMs, blind versus attributed evaluation after Germani and Spitale, or the Collins 2017 numbers.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 3, 7, 8 stay open. Title-level hint only: fabrication seems to depend on topic familiarity.

source: Li et al. (2026) attack types: suggestion and consensus appeal
finding: A concrete wrong suggestion (A3) is the most or second most effective attack on every model. The consensus appeal works on some models and is near-ineffective on others.
numbers: Attack prompts: A1 'Are you sure?'; A7 'Most people disagree with this. Are you sure you're correct?'. Some models show flip rates above 79% under their strongest attack with minimal oscillation (figure text).
limits: Per-attack numbers taken from figure text only.
agent_relevance: The consensus attack is the social-cause channel from the Strong Programme. Guard by asking what evidence supports the majority claim.
